title: Trustworthy AI Helper - Design & Test the Data (Part 1 Core)
summary: Students design a small AI helper from three parts - a task, a structured prompt and data - then run a clean-versus-noisy data test and explain how data quality changed the output.
objectives: Design a small prompt-driven AI helper: state the task, the structured prompt, and the data it will use.
Test how the quality of the data changes the helper's output, and explain the effect.

body: Over four lessons (two weeks, Core and Lab) you will build a **Trustworthy AI Helper** and prove it can be trusted.
Today you design it and test how the data quality changes its output.

sections.heading: I can…
items: I can design a helper with a clear task, a structured prompt, and a data set.
I can test how data quality changes the output and explain why.

terms.definition: A small AI solution that completes a task using a prompt and data.
A precise instruction: goal, details, and the form of the answer.
How accurate, balanced, and complete the data is.

sections.heading: A helper has three parts
body: A [[helper]] is a small solution: a task, a structured prompt, and data.
Its output comes from the data and the prompt, so if the data is poor, the output is poor - even with a good prompt.

sections.label: The three parts you are designing
sections.heading: A helper has three parts
sections.altText: A bar split into three parts — the data it uses, the prompt that drives it, and the checks that catch mistakes — which together make a helper you can trust.

parts.label: Its prompt
parts.detail: what you ask it to do

sections.caption: All three are yours to design. **A helper with no checks is not finished** — it is a helper you are hoping about.

sections.heading: Test the data quality
body: Feed your helper clean data, then noisy data, and compare the outputs.
This shows how much the [[data quality]] matters. Poorer data usually gives a poorer, less fair output.

sections.label: Let's try it - hands-on
body: Design your helper, then test clean vs noisy data.
items: Run on clean data; note the output.
Run on noisy data; note the output.

sections.heading: Think about it
items: Why is a good prompt not enough on its own?
How did the noisy data change your output?
What will you build in the Lab?

worksheet.title: Week 5 - Core - Worksheet | Trustworthy AI Helper - Design & Test the Data (Part 1 Core)

questions.prompt: Layla's helper has one task: recommend a library book for her class. She has the class reading survey as her data. Which of these is the best structured prompt for that task?

options.text: Using our class reading survey, suggest one book most of the class would enjoy, and give one sentence saying why.
Using our class reading survey, suggest some books people might like.
Suggest one book and write as much as you possibly can about it, in as much detail as you can manage.

feedback.correct: That prompt gives the goal, the details (which data to use) and the form of the answer, so the helper knows exactly what to produce.
feedback.incorrect: A structured prompt needs all three: the goal, the details such as which data to use, and the form the answer should take - being longer or politer is not the same as being structured.

questions.prompt: Layla's finished helper is described below. Match each part of her description to the part of the helper it is.

left.text: Recommend one library book that most of the class would enjoy
Using the class reading survey, name one book and give one sentence saying why
'The Lost Ship' - because 19 pupils chose adventure stories

feedback.correct: A helper is a task, a structured prompt and data - and what comes back out of it is the output, not one of its parts.
feedback.incorrect: The task is the job to be done, the data is what the helper reads, the structured prompt is the instruction you write, and the output is what the helper gives back.

questions.prompt: Sami's survey data has several entries typed in twice and a few answers copied into the wrong column. He rewrites his prompt so it is very precise. True or false: the precise prompt will make up for the messy data, so the output can be trusted.

feedback.correct: Right - the output is built from the data as well as the prompt, so poor data still gives a poor output however precise the wording is.
feedback.incorrect: A prompt only tells the helper what to do with the data it is given; if the data is wrong, a better-worded instruction cannot invent the right answer.

questions.prompt: Put the steps of a clean-versus-noisy data test in the order you would carry them out.

items.text: Write the task your helper must do.
Write the structured prompt and prepare the clean data.
Run the helper on the clean data and note the output.
Run the same prompt on the noisy version of the data and note the output.
Compare the two outputs and explain how the data quality caused the difference.

feedback.correct: Keeping the prompt the same and changing only the data is what makes the difference in the outputs fair to blame on data quality.
feedback.incorrect: Design first, then run the clean data, then run the very same prompt on the noisy data - only then can you compare and explain the difference.

questions.prompt: Kareem's helper recommends whichever genre the most survey responses chose. His clean survey has 20 responses: 11 chose adventure and 9 chose sport. By mistake, some of the sport responses are copied and counted again. What is the smallest number of copied sport responses that would make the helper recommend sport instead of adventure?

feedback.correct: Three copies take sport from 9 to 12, just past adventure's 11 - a handful of duplicated rows is enough to flip the recommendation.
feedback.incorrect: Sport needs more than adventure's 11, and two copies only make it 11, which is a tie - so it takes three copies to overturn the real result.

formative.targets: Integrated mastery - CU (data quality affects outputs) and SD (design a promptdriven solution)
formative.check: Helper design planner + clean-vs-noisy data test reviewed against the mastery criteria
